reviews.review: Wish they did a Space Marine 2 instead of the failure that is Eternal Crusade :(

I bought this game a long time ago, when it came out for PS3. At first I didn't like it at all, I was playing the Italian version and the voiceover was completely out of sync. I bought it on Steam a few days ago, and decided I had to finish it no matter what.
I really enjoyed this game, although it has some flaws.
Here is what I think of Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine.
Please note that this review is based on the Hard difficulty setting, for that is the one I played in Single Player.
I will not cover the multiplayer, as I haven't spent enough time there.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]
The game features an old school, very linear campaign. You simply walk straight to your objective, leaving a trail of dead bodies behind you. You have a set of ranged weapons and a few close-combat options, plus the Fury mode which allows you to become a badass for a while. You cannot upgrade your weapons and skills by spending points or anything like this; instead, you will find different weapons lying around - some can be permanently replaced by superior models - and Purity Seals which give some permanent boost to your Fury.
It's not a system I'm really fond of, but it seems to work okay. You will be able to switch to different weapons almost at any time, so you can try them all and see what you prefer.
There also are some collectables around, you will find them interesting if you care about the characters and their stories, and 60 Steam Achievements.

[h1]GRAPHICS[/h1]
This game isn't anything special graphics-wise. Models are good, but some textures aren't great and most environments seem a little too empty. I think every enemy class has a single model. It's not a very big deal, but some variety could be nice.

[h1]SOUND[/h1]
The voices and sound effects are pretty solid, but I was expecting something more from the Orks. Some more lines for all enemies in general would have been a nice touch.

[h1]DIFFICULTY[/h1]
The game is not really hard, I finished it in around 10 hours in Hard mode and only died a few times. There are, in my opinion, only three or four sections that are actually hard, and that's because of the enemy spawnpoints: they will be able to hit you from any angle, so sometimes you just rely on luck or finding the glitchy spot they can't hit.


[h1]IN CONCLUSION[/h1]
Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a nice game, and you can get it for a very affordable price. It's a little bit different from what we're used nowdays, but it still offers a nice level of challenge and entertainment. If you enjoy Warhammer 40,000 games, you will probably enjoy Space Marine too.

Think "Gears of War" meets "Darksiders" set in the Warhammer 40k universe.

Edit: I recently replayed this game on easy mode after having originally beat it on hard and I know believe that is the ideal mode to play this game, as it truly allows the player to feel like an overpowered space marine while still allowing difficulty spikes to sneak up on you and force you to change tactics without killing the pacing or requiring you to resort to cheap methods. Most of the following criticisms are invalid in the easy mode.

 A brutal, meaty hack-n-slash, 3rd person shooter hybrid unfortunately marred throughout by questionable design choices and generic game conventions.

You play as Captain Titus, the titular space marine as he fights to turn back the tides of space orks and daemons invading an industrial world. There is a small variety of guns, melee weapons, and upgrades to be found throughout the levels. Also, as you kill you build up a meter that allows you to go into a "rage mode" for a while that increases your damage and heals you. Also, stunning enemies allows you to perform contextual executions that also replenish your health. Standard, but serviceable fare.

At its best, I had a lot of fun slaughtering orks, traitor marines, and daemons with the melee combat, and I found the shooting to be cathartic enough when used sparingly. The melee combat is supremely satisfying, with a number of hard-hitting combos and brutal executions. Also, the sections with the jump pack are some of the funnest moments I've ever had in any game. However, there are several things to this game that might make or break the experience for you. 

First of all, the levels: virtually every single level is a dirt brown industrial complex with little variation. A counter I hear to this is that this is in the "grim-dark" 40k universe, so it is to be expected, but I know for a fact that the 40k universe has some of the most diverse locales of any fictional setting, a fact this game does not take advantage of.  

Second, the enemy variety leaves a lot to be desired. The types of Orks found in the game are the same as of any game: light, standard, heavy, ranged, melee, heavy melee. This in and of itself isn't the worst thing, but level after level has you fighting wave upon wave of the same orks and the same ork types with little variation or sense of pacing. When the forces of Chaos arrived, it was a welcomed change of pacing, until I realized they were the exact same enemy types as the orks, with only a skin change. 

Also, to hell with the exploding squigs that kill you with one or two hits. They make sense in a shooter, but they have no place in a hack and slash game. I can't count the number of times my fun slaughtering orcs with a thunder hammer or chain sword was ruined by a parade of exploding squigs that forced me to stop enjoying the game and instead hide in the far corner of the level trying to pick them off at a distance amongst a sea of orks. Oh what fun. Completely ruins the illusion of being an ultra-powerful space marine.

My biggest gripe with the game is also one of its biggest draws: the weapons systems. The 40k universe is famous for its variety of extremely bombastic and overpowered weaponry, but this game takes these weapons and reduces them to the same basic, standard weaponry found in every game. The bolter becomes a machine gun, the melta gun: a shotgun. To its credit, the enemies do disappear into a fine, red mist when killed, but they are so bullet-spongy that you might as well be throwing pieces of the scenery at them than shooting them. 

The worst part of the generic weapon system is the limited inventory. You can only carry four weapons at a time, and you don't get to choose which slots switch out with which weapon. Meaning: you can't have a sniper rifle and a scatter gun at the same time, but you are stuck with the pistol for the entire game. Are you telling me that Doomguy can carry an arsenal of every weapon known to man but an Ultramarine can only carry four weapons? 

Also, weapon upgrades coincide with enemy upgrades, meaning that you never notice your weapons getting any more powerful. On top of that, many weapon upgrades take shape in alternative weapons that give more damage, but have a ridiculously low amount of ammo or long reload time. Why is this? Shouldn't more powerful weapons make me feel more powerful? 

Worst of all, in wielding the most powerful melee weapon in the game, you can only use your pistol and bolter, ie your weakest weapons. This wouldn't be so bad if the game let you choose an emphasis on either melee or ranged combat, but instead it will often provide you with the mighty thunder hammer, close the door behind you, autosave, and then force you into a sniping section with only your pistol and bolter to defend yourself. Simply infuriating, and disincentivizes you to choose one of the most powerful weapons in the game. 

For a game about being a spacemarine, this game strongly discourages you from feeling like one. The game mechanics are at constant war with the source material.

The best aspect of this game is far and beyond the story. Against the yawn-inducing backdrops are an incredible cast of characters with superb voice acting that truly bring the sense of doom and despair inherent in an invasion and makes the player feel a part of the stifling, grim 40k universe. The writing has a suprising amount of depth, exploring themes such as autonomy vs discipline, perfect for a setting that takes both to the extreme, but without marring the progression of the plot. 

All in all, a solid game with extremely frustrating conventional mechanics. A must-have for 40k fans, but might not be for everyone.

The game itself is a wild ride from start to finish, and is a great way to show off the power and training of the Adeptus Astartes, even if the game follows [strike] Matt Ward's biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥ [/strike] arguably the worst Chapter in all of the 40k Universe. Thankfully, Captain Titus makes it bearable.

Buy the game when it's on sale, sit back and enjoy the mindless slaughter of this grimdark universe.

Quite fun in the beginning but after a while features way too many ranged attacks that forces you to take cover and take pot shots at the enemies rather than indulge in the fun close quarters combat. Also not as responsive in its movement as I'd like. Have no shame in playng the game on easy as the most fun (I found) is in mindlessly fighting through the ork horde and not dying 5 seconds after entering combat because you couldn't find cover in time (and this game does not have a cover system, you just gotta stand behind cover that's tall enough). 

Can reecommend on sale only.
